intro: In this college you'll learn how to get around the Netherlands: name the ways you travel, tell the time, ask what time a train leaves, read a timetable, politely ask a stranger for help, apologise when you are late, and ask for directions.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — how do you travel?
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme six. Its title is [[Hoe reis jij?]], which means 'how do you travel?'. In the Netherlands you move around a lot, so this theme is very practical. Let's start with the main ways to travel. The verb 'to travel' is [[reizen]], and you usually say how you go with the little word [[met]], meaning 'by'. So you can travel [[met de trein]], by train; [[met de bus]], by bus; [[met de tram]], by tram; [[met de fiets]], by bike; or [[met de auto]], by car. To say it in a full sentence, you say [[Ik ga met de bus naar mijn werk.]], which means 'I go to work by bus'. Notice the word order: first the means of transport, then where you go. If you walk, you say [[Ik ga te voet.]], 'I go on foot', or simply [[Ik ga lopend.]] A small culture note: the Netherlands is famous for its bikes, and almost everyone owns a [[fiets]]. People cycle to work, to school, and to the shops, rain or shine. So if a neighbour asks [[Hoe reis jij naar je werk?]], a very Dutch answer is [[Ik ga met de fiets.]] Let's keep going!

paragraphs.heading: Telling the time
paragraphs.text: To travel, you need the time. The question is [[Hoe laat is het?]], which means 'what time is it?'. For full hours you add the word [[uur]], 'o'clock', like this: [[Het is drie uur.]], 'it is three o'clock'. For half hours, Dutch does something surprising: [[half]] points to the NEXT hour. So [[half vier]] is not half past four — it is 3:30. Say it slowly with me: [[Het is half vier.]] For the quarters, use [[kwart over]] for 'quarter past' and [[kwart voor]] for 'quarter to'. So 7:15 is [[kwart over zeven]], and 1:45 is [[kwart voor twee]]. For minutes you use [[over]], 'past', and [[voor]], 'to': ten to six is [[tien voor zes]]. Now, the most useful travel question of all is [[Hoe laat gaat de trein?]], meaning 'what time does the train go?'. You will also hear [[Hoe laat vertrekt de bus?]], 'what time does the bus leave?'. To say at what time, use the little word [[om]]: [[De trein gaat om negen uur.]], 'the train goes at nine o'clock'. Practise your daily routine too: [[Ik sta om zeven uur op.]] means 'I get up at seven'. Times feel tricky at first, so say them out loud every day.

paragraphs.heading: Separable verbs: leaving, changing, arriving
paragraphs.text: Travelling brings four very important verbs, and three of them are 'separable', which means a little front part jumps to the end of the sentence. Don't worry, I'll show you. The verb [[vertrekken]] means 'to leave' or 'to depart', and it stays together: [[De trein vertrekt om tien uur.]], 'the train leaves at ten'. But [[aankomen]], 'to arrive', splits: the [[aan]] jumps to the end, so you say [[Ik kom om elf uur aan.]], 'I arrive at eleven'. The verb [[overstappen]] means 'to change' or 'to transfer', and it also splits: [[Ik stap in Utrecht over.]], 'I change in Utrecht'. And [[uitstappen]] means 'to get off', so [[Ik stap bij het station uit.]] means 'I get off at the station'. A handy test: put the verb in an 'I' sentence. If a little part flies to the end, the verb is separable. So a real travel sentence might be [[Ik vertrek om acht uur en kom om half tien aan.]], meaning 'I leave at eight and arrive at half past nine'. These four verbs come up constantly on trains and buses, so repeat them now: [[vertrekken, aankomen, overstappen, uitstappen]]. You'll hear them in every station announcement.

paragraphs.heading: Tickets, timetables and the OV-chipkaart
paragraphs.text: Now let's get you onto the train. The Dutch railway company is called [[de NS]], short for Nederlandse Spoorwegen. The timetable is [[de dienstregeling]], and the platform is [[het perron]]. A ticket is [[een kaartje]], and to buy one you can say [[Een kaartje naar Rotterdam, alstublieft.]], 'a ticket to Rotterdam, please'. But most people don't buy paper tickets at all. Instead they use a travel card called the [[OV-chipkaart]], which works on the train, the bus, the tram and the metro across the whole country. The clever part: you must check in and check out by holding your card against a reader. Listen for the announcements [[Vergeet niet in te checken.]], 'don't forget to check in', and [[Vergeet niet uit te checken.]], 'don't forget to check out'. If you forget to check out, you pay too much, so this really matters. At the station you'll want two more questions: [[Op welk perron staat de trein?]], 'which platform is the train on?', and [[Moet ik overstappen?]], 'do I have to change?'. If there's a delay, you'll hear [[De trein heeft tien minuten vertraging.]], 'the train is ten minutes delayed'. The word [[vertraging]] means 'delay', and on a busy day in the Netherlands you'll hear it a lot.

paragraphs.heading: Asking a stranger politely — and being late
paragraphs.text: Sometimes you need to ask a stranger for help, and Dutch has a polite, gentle way to start. You say [[Pardon, mag ik u iets vragen?]], which means 'excuse me, may I ask you something?'. Notice the polite word [[u]] for 'you' — always use it with people you don't know. Another soft opener is [[Sorry dat ik u stoor.]], 'sorry to bother you'. Then you can ask your question, for example [[Weet u hoe laat de trein vertrekt?]], 'do you know what time the train leaves?'. When someone helps you, thank them warmly: [[Dank u wel voor uw hulp!]], 'thank you very much for your help', and they'll often reply [[Graag gedaan!]], 'you're welcome'. Now, life happens and sometimes you're late. The Dutch value being on time, so a quick apology goes a long way. You can say [[Sorry dat ik te laat ben.]], 'sorry that I'm late', and add a reason like [[De bus reed niet.]], 'the bus didn't run', or [[Er was veel vertraging.]], 'there was a lot of delay'. To reassure someone, say [[Ik ben er over tien minuten.]], 'I'll be there in ten minutes'. And a lovely Dutch saying fits perfectly here: [[Beter laat dan nooit.]], 'better late than never'.

paragraphs.heading: Asking directions — a mini-scenario
paragraphs.text: Finally, directions. The key words are short and easy: [[links]] means 'left', [[rechts]] means 'right', and [[rechtdoor]] means 'straight ahead'. To ask the way, say [[Hoe kom ik bij het station?]], 'how do I get to the station?', or [[Waar is de dichtstbijzijnde bushalte?]], 'where is the nearest bus stop?'. An answer might be [[Ga rechtdoor en dan de eerste straat links.]], 'go straight ahead and then the first street on the left'. Now picture it. You arrive in a new town and you're a little lost. You stop a friendly stranger and say: [[Pardon, mag ik u iets vragen?]] [[Hoe kom ik bij het centrum?]] The stranger smiles and answers: [[Ga hier rechtdoor, bij de stoplichten gaat u rechts, en dan ziet u het centrum.]] You say [[Is het ver lopen?]], 'is it a long walk?', and they reply [[Nee, ongeveer vijf minuten.]], 'no, about five minutes'. You finish with [[Dank u wel!]] and they wish you [[Goede reis!]], 'have a good trip'. See? You just travelled across a Dutch town using only this theme. You're doing brilliantly. [[Heel goed gedaan, en tot de volgende keer!]] Well done, and see you next time!
